atoms.text: `research/` — documentation only: assays, notes, designs, findings. No buildable code.
`nursery/` — all software: prototypes, tools, scripts, experiments. One directory per project.
`vendor/` — third-party clones used as research sources (git-ignored).

Code written into `nursery/<name>/` gets a symlink from the motivating `research/<topic>/` doc (e.g. `cargo-gpui -> ../../nursery/cargo-gpui`) plus a one-line pointer near the top: "Prototype at `nursery/<name>/`".
Nurseries self-contained: own `Cargo.toml`/README stating what it is and which research doc it belongs to.
Research references code through the symlink path, not `nursery/` directly.
Research dirs stay greppable, publishable prose — no target dirs, no lockfiles.
Code stays buildable and isolated in nursery; graduates to its own repo without dragging research along.
`cargo check` for fast iteration; `cargo build` and `cargo test` to verify.
`cargo clippy` before done; `cargo fmt` on changed files.
Respect `rust-toolchain.toml` MSRV when present.
Binary thin, library fat: logic in lib modules, testable without the CLI.
Workspace for multi-crate; one concern per crate.
Prefer std and small maintained crates; pin with `=` only for engines or audited releases.
Use the package manager matching the lockfile: pnpm-lock.yaml → pnpm, yarn.lock → yarn, else npm.
TypeScript: `tsc --noEmit` before done; tests via the repo's configured runner.
Lockfile committed, node_modules never.
Scripts in package.json are the interface: build, test, lint.
`agents:` — add the instruction that follows to this AGENTS.md, then commit the change. E.g. `agents: always commit after finishing a logical unit of work`.

`ac:` — "add command": register a new command in this section, then commit the change. Form: `ac: <word>: <what it does>`; afterwards the command is invoked as `<word>:` in messages. E.g. `ac: log: append a dated line to docs/log.md`.

`vendor:` — clone the given repos (one or more URLs or local paths, space-separated) into `./vendor/`, then commit the change. Use for third-party sources kept as research references. E.g. `vendor: https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF ../other/repo`.

`fv:` — fork the given repo(s) with `gh` and clone the fork into `./vendor/`, then commit the change. If `gh` is not installed, ask the user before installing it. E.g. `fv: https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_rust.git`.
`sv:` — shallow clone (`git clone --depth 1`) the given repo(s) into `./vendor/`, then commit the change. E.g. `sv: https://github.com/gastownhall/beads.git`.

`s:` — status: check the status of this repository (git state, cursors in `features.md`, recent commits) and get up to speed on where things stand. Read-only; no commit. When the scene-mcp MCP tools are available in the session, also call `get_viewer_logs` to check what the browser viewer has been reporting and `get_viewer_photos` to see if the user uploaded reference photos (then `get_viewer_photo` to view one).
Always commit after finishing a logical unit of work (coding, documentation, etc).

**`features.md`** is the feature queue. It is *append-only, check-off, move the cursor*: 1. New ideas get appended to the bottom of the Queue, one entry per feature: checkbox, sequence number, one-line description, acceptance criteria, milestone tag if it belongs to one. 2. Slots are ordered by implementation order — slot an entry into place only *before* work starts. Once the cursor passes an item, don't reorder above it. 3. Work strictly top-down from the cursor (`◀ HERE`). 4. On completion: check the box, move the cursor down, keep the entry (it becomes the record that the feature shipped).

**`docs/architecture.md`** is the living description of what is built. Update it *when implementing a feature that changes* the data model, id scheme, extras mapping, tool surface, or crate layering — not after the fact. It reflects reality, never the plan.
**README.md** Status/Milestone lines track the coarse milestone position only (M0–M5); detail lives in the two docs above.
**Research doc** (`research/scene-mcp/README.md`, parent repo): update only for decisions, not implementation progress.

Nothing user-visible awaits the network. Any HTTP/socket call on a render path (telemetry, catalog fetch, update check) runs on a background worker; the paint path hands the work off and returns immediately. Delivery semantics (timeout, retry, ordering) live with the worker, not the caller.

Telemetry is fire-and-forget from user-facing code. `pa-telemetry`'s background worker owns delivery end to end; no startup, session create, tab open, or first-render path may hold a flush or await a sink.
Fire-and-forget boundaries need a red-first test: a hanging sink (one that never replies) must not delay paint. The test fails if any await on the critical path reaches the worker's delivery.
Tests that mock a sink or run offline cannot prove the above (the benchmark's mock hides the POST). The regression test with a hanging sink is the required verifier.

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace` must pass before every merge. Run `make check` — the local mirror of the same gates; CI runs on the org's billing (`.github/workflows/continuous.yml` on `main` pushes; `release.yml` on version tags). The PR-only codebase-health check reports growth past 2,000 lines as review guidance; it never blocks a merge.

**Parity-diff evidence is a merge gate** (the port's definition, not optional polish): every PR that touches a user-visible surface must include a "parity-diff evidence" section in its description showing the TS-binary comparison for what it changed: (1) rendered output — frame-diff vs the TS binary; (2) interactive behavior — the same input handled identically (keys, mouse, timing); (3) wire parity — byte-compare the TS daemon's traffic for protocol changes; (4) user-visible invariants — every user action produces the same visible reaction as TS (`/compact` shows started+completed; `/model` shows the selector; a refinement shows its decoration). A feature that "works" but was never diffed against the TS binary does not pass review. If TS shows it, Rust shows it identically; if Rust shows something TS does not, that is also a parity bug.

PRs must state ownership compliance (crate README scope/non-goals/public API, dependency direction) and classify the change: internals, new `pub` surface, or a new dependency/cross-crate re-export. The latter two are architectural changes — an innocent-looking `pub use` is a very simple way to break encapsulation.

GLB reader color support: COLOR_0 is read as F32 VEC4, or F32 VEC3 promoted to RGBA (alpha 1.0); other encodings (normalized u8/u16) are skipped, never misread — see read_colors in src/parsers/glb.rs.
